passages.source_text: ταῦτα τοῦ Πέτρου εἰπόντος ἐπιστήσασα ὡς ὑπὸ ἐκπλήξεως ἀπέψυξεν ἡ γυνή. ὁ δὲ Πέτρος προσελθὼν καὶ ἐπισχὼν νήφειν αὐτὴν παρεκελεύσατο, ὁμολογεῖν αὐτὴν πείθων τί ποτε ἔστιν ὃ πάσχει. ἡ δὲ ὥσπερ ἐκ μέθης τὸ λοιπὸν τοῦ σώματος παρεθεῖσα ὑπέστρεψεν ἑαυτὴν ὑποστῆναι δυνηθῆναι τὸ μέγεθος τῆς ἐλπιζομένης χαρᾶς, καὶ τρίψασα αὐτῆς τὸ πρόσωπον Ποῦ ἔστιν (ἔφη) οὗτος ὁ νεανίας; ὁ δὲ ἤδη ὅλον συνιδὼν τὸ πρᾶγμα ἔφη Εἰπέ μοι σὺ πρῶτον (ἄλλως γὰρ τοῦτον ἰδεῖν οὐκ ἔχεις) —. ἡ δὲ σπεύδουσα Ἐγώ (φησίν) εἰμι ἡ τοῦ νεανίσκου μήτηρ. καὶ ὁ Πέτρος ἔφη Τί τούτῳ ὄνομα; ἡ δέ φησιν Κλήμης. καὶ ὁ Πέτρος εἶπεν Αὐτός ἐστιν, καὶ αὐτὸς ἦν ὁ πρὸ μικροῦ μοι λαλήσας, ᾧ ἀναμένειν με ἐν τῷ πλοίῳ προσέταξα. ἡ δὲ προσπεσοῦσα τῷ Πέτρῳ παρεκάλει σπεύδειν ἐπὶ τὸ πλοῖον ἐλθεῖν. καὶ ὁ Πέτρος Εἴ μοι τηρεῖς τὰς συνθήκας, καὶ τοῦτο ποιήσω. ἡ δὲ ἔφη Πάντα ποιῶ, μόνον μοι τὸ τέκνον τὸ μονογενὲς δεῖξον· δόξω γὰρ δι’ αὐτοῦ τὰ δύο μου τὰ ἐνταῦθα τεθνηκότα ὁρᾶν τέκνα. καὶ ὁ Πέτρος ἔφη Ὅταν αὐτὸν ἴδῃς, ἡσύχασον μέχρις ἂν τῆς νήσου ἐκβῶμεν. ἡ δὲ ἔφη Οὕτως ποιήσω.

λαβόμενος οὖν τῆς χειρὸς αὐτῆς ὁ Πέτρος ἦγεν ἐπὶ τὸ πλοῖον. ἐγὼ δὲ ἰδὼν αὐτὸν χειραγωγοῦντα γυναῖκα ἐγέλασα, καὶ προσελθὼν εἰς τιμὴν αὐτοῦ ἀντ’ αὐτοῦ χειραγωγεῖν αὐτὴν ἐπειρώμην. καὶ ἅμα τῷ ἅψασθαί με τῆς χειρὸς αὐτῆς ὀλολύξασα ὡς μήτηρ μέγα καὶ περιπλακεῖσα σφόδρα κατεφίλει με τὸν αὐτῆς υἱόν. ἐγὼ δὲ ἀγνοῶν ὅλον τὸ πρᾶγμα ὡς μαινομένην ἀπεσειόμην, αἰδούμενος δὲ καὶ τὸν Πέτρον ἐπικραινόμην.

ὁ δὲ Πέτρος ἔφη Ἔα· τί ποιεῖς, τέκνον Κλήμης, ἀποσειόμενος τὴν σὴν ὄντως τεκοῦσαν; ἐγὼ δὲ τοῦτο ἀκούσας περίδακρυς γενόμενος καὶ καταπεσούσῃ τῇ τεκούσῃ προσπεσὼν κατεφίλουν. καὶ γὰρ ἅμα τῷ ῥηθῆναί μοι τοῦτο ἀμαυρῶς πως τὸ εἶδος ἀνεκαλούμην. πολλοὶ μὲν οὖν ὄχλοι συνέτρεχον ἱστορῆσαι τὴν προσαιτήτριαν γυναῖκα, λέγοντες ἀλλήλοις ὅτι αὐτὴν ἐπέγνω ὁ υἱός, ἀνὴρ ἀξιόλογος. βουλομένοις οὖν ἡμῖν ἐξαυτῆς σὺν τῇ μητρὶ τῆς νήσου ἐκβαίνειν ἡ μήτηρ ἔφη Τέκνον μοι ποθεινόν, εὔλογόν ἐστιν ἀποτάξασθαι τῇ ὑποδεξαμένῃ με γυναικί, ἥτις πενιχρὰ οὖσα καὶ ὅλη παρειμένη ἐπὶ τῆς οἰκίας ἔρριπται. ὁ δὲ Πέτρος ἀκούσας ἐθαύμασεν καὶ πάντες οἱ περιεστῶτες ὄχλοι τῆς γυναικὸς τὸ ἀγαθὸν φρόνημα. καὶ εὐθέως ἐκέλευσεν ὁ Πέτρος τισὶν πορευθῆναι καὶ τὴν γυναῖκα ἐπὶ κλίνης κομίσαι. καὶ ὁμῶς ἐνεχθείσης καὶ τεθείσης τῆς κλίνης, πάντων τῶν ὄχλων ἀκουόντων ἔφη ὁ Πέτρος. Εἰ ἀληθείας κῆρυξ ἐγὼ τυγχάνω, εἰς τὴν τῶν παρεστώτων πίστιν, ἵνα γνῶσιν ὅτι εἷς ἐστιν θεὸς ὁ τὸν κόσμον ποιήσας, ἐξαυτῆς ἐγερθήτω ὑγιής. καὶ ἅμα τῷ εἰπεῖν Πέτρον ταῦτα ἡ γυνὴ ἠγέρθη ὑγιασθεῖσα καὶ τῷ Πέτρῳ προσέπεσεν καὶ τὴν συνήθη φίλην καταφιλήσασα ἐπυνθάνετο τί εἴη τοῦτο. ἡ δὲ ὅλον αὐτῇ τὸ πρᾶγμα τοῦ ἀναγνωρισμοῦ συντόμως διηγήσατο καὶ οἱ ἀκούσαντες κατεπλάγησαν. τότε καὶ ἡ μήτηρ τὴν ξενοδόχον θεραπευθεῖσαν ἱστορήσασα παρεκάλει καὶ αὐτὴ ἰάσεως τυχεῖν. ὁ δὲ ἐπιθεὶς τὴν χεῖρα καὶ αὐτὴν ἐθεράπευσεν.

καὶ εἶθ’ οὕτως ὁ Πέτρος περὶ θεοῦ καὶ τῆς αὐτῷ διαφερούσης θρησκείας ὁμιλήσας, προσθεὶς ἐπὶ τέλει ὅτι Εἴ τις βούλεται ταῦτα ἀκριβῶς μαθεῖν, εἰς Ἀντιόχειαν, ὅπου πλειόνων ἡμερῶν περιμένειν ἔκρινα, ἐλθὼν τὰ πρὸς τὴν αὐτοῦ σωτηρίαν μανθανέτω. οὐ γὰρ δὴ ἐμπορίας ἕνεκα ἢ στρατείας πατρίδας καταλιμπάνειν οἴδατε καὶ εἰς μακροὺς ἀπέρχεσθαι τόπους, διὰ δὲ αἰώνιον σωτηρίαν μηδὲ τριῶν ἡμερῶν ὁδὸν πορευθῆναι θέλειν. μετὰ μὲν οὖν τὴν προσομιλίαν Πέτρου ἐγὼ τῇ ὑγιασθείσῃ γυναικὶ ἐπὶ παντὸς τοῦ ὄχλου χιλίας δραχμὰς εἰς τροφὰς ἐδωρησάμην, παραθέμενος αὐτὴν ἀγαθῷ τινὶ ἀνδρί, πρώτῳ τῆς πόλεως ὄντι, φύσει μετὰ χαρᾶς τοῦτο ποιεῖν προῃρημένῳ. ἔτι δὲ καὶ ἄλλοις πολλοῖς ἀργύρια διανείμας, ταῖς ποτὲ τὴν μητέρα παραμυθησαμέναις εὐχαριστήσας διέπλευσα εἰς Ἀντάραδον ἅμα τῇ μητρὶ καὶ Πέτρῳ καὶ τοῖς λοιποῖς ἑταίροις, καὶ οὕτως εἰς τὴν ξενίαν ὡρμήσαμεν.

γενομένων δὲ ἡμῶν ... καὶ τροφῆς μεταλαβόντων καὶ συνήθως εὐχαριστησάντων, ἔτι ὥρας οὔσης ἔφην ἐγὼ τῷ Πέτρῳ Φιλανθρωπίας ἔργον, κύριέ μου Πέτρε, ἡ ἐμὴ ἐποίησεν μήτηρ, τῆς ξενοδόχου ὑπομνησθεῖσα γυναικός. καὶ ὁ Πέτρος ἀπεκρίνατο Ἆρά γε, ὦ Κλήμης, ἀληθῶς νενόμικας φιλανθρωπίας ἔργον πεποιηκέναι τὴν σὴν τεκοῦσαν, καθὸ τὴν ἀπὸ ναυφραγίου αὐτὴν ὑποδεξαμένην ἠμείψατο, ἢ ὡς μητρὶ μεγάλα χαριζόμενος τοῦτον εἴρηκας τὸν λόγον; εἰ δὲ οὐχ ὡς χαριζόμενος, ἀλλ’ ὡς ἀληθεύων ἔφης, ἔοικάς μοι ἀγνοεῖν τί ποτ’ ἔστιν φιλανθρωπίας μέγεθος, ἥτις ἐστὶν ἡ ἄνευ τοῦ φυσικῶς πείθοντος πρὸς οἱονδήποτε στοργὴ καθὸ ἄνθρωπός ἐστιν. ἀλλ’ οὐδὲ τὴν ξενοδόχον τὴν ἀπὸ ναυφραγίου ὑποδεξαμένην τὴν σὴν τεκοῦσαν οὕτω φιλάνθρωπον εἰπεῖν τολμῶ. ὑπ’ ἐλέου γὰρ κολακευθεῖσα πέπειστο εὐεργέτις γενέσθαι γυναικὸς ναυφραγίῳ περιπεσούσης, τέκνα πενθούσης, ξένης, γυμνῆς, μεμονωμένης καὶ σφόδρα ἐπὶ ταῖς συμφοραῖς ὀλοφυρομένης. ἐν τοσαύταις οὖν αὐτῆς συμφοραῖς οὔσης, τίς καὶ ἀσεβῶν ἰδὼν οὐκ ἂν ἠλέησεν; ὥστε οὕτω φιλανθρωπίας ἔργον πεποιηκυῖα φαίνεται οὐδὲ ἡ ξενοδόχος γυνή, ἀλλὰ ὑπὸ ἐλέου τοῦ ἐπὶ μυρίαις συμφοραῖς πρὸς εὐεργεσίας κεκινημένου. πόσῳ γε μᾶλλον ἡ σὴ τεκοῦσα, βίου εὐπορέσασα καὶ τὴν ξενοδόχον ἀμειψαμένη, φιλανθρωπίας. ἔργον οὐκ ἐποίησεν, ἀλλὰ φιλίας; πολλὴ δὲ διαφορὰ μεταξὺ φιλίας καὶ φιλανθρωπίας, ὅτι ἡ μὲν φιλία ἐξ ἀμοιβῆς γίνεται, ἡ δὲ φιλανθρωπία ἄνευ τοῦ φυσικῶς πείθοντος πάντα ἄνθρωπον καθὸ ἄνθρωπός ἐστιν φιλοῦσα εὐεργετεῖ. εἰ μὲν οὖν ἡ ἐλεήσασα ξενοδόχος καὶ ἐχθροὺς ἀδικήσαντας ἐλεῶσα εὐεργέτει, φιλάνθρωπος ἂν. ἦν. εἰ δὲ διὰ τί φίλη ἡ ἐχθρὰ καὶ διὰ τί ἐχθρὰ ἡ φίλη, ἡ τοιαύτη τοῦ τινὸς αἰτίου φίλη ἐστὶν ἢ ἐχθρά, οὐ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου.

context.translation_policy_text:
# Translation Stance

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Contested terms

The following terms appear frequently and carry heavy theological
weight. Our default rendering and rationale are recorded here.
Per-verse variance is documented in the individual YAML files.

| Greek / Hebrew | Default English | Alternatives considered | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Χριστός *Christos* | Messiah where independently titular; Christ in the name forms "Jesus Christ" / "Christ Jesus" | Christ, Messiah | Preserves the title's Hebraic messianic meaning while using the recognizable conventional English personal name |
| κύριος *Kyrios* | Lord | LORD, Master | Matches covenantal and NT usage |
| δοῦλος *doulos* | servant | bondservant, slave | Uses reader-facing "servant" consistently; documents bonded-status and ownership nuance in notes/audit metadata |
| πίστις *pistis* | faith | faithfulness, trust | Main text: faith; footnote alternatives where contested |
| δικαιοσύνη *dikaiosynē* | righteousness | justice | Both renderings preserved in footnotes for Pauline passages |
| ἱλαστήριον *hilastērion* | atoning sacrifice | propitiation, mercy seat | Dynamic rendering for accessibility; alternatives footnoted |
| ἀγάπη *agapē* | love | charity (archaic) | Lexical cognates in source kept |
| σάρξ *sarx* | flesh (literal) / sinful nature (metaphorical) | — | Context-dependent; per-verse documented |
| μετανοέω / μετάνοια *metanoeō / metanoia* | reorient / reorientation; toward God where the context warrants making the destination explicit | repent / repentance (traditional); reconsider / change of mind in documented exceptions | See "Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)" below; do not homogenize regret, divine relenting, or distinct turning words |
| νήφω *nēphō* | clear-minded (most contexts); sober (where Paul explicitly runs the drunk/sober metaphor) | sober-minded | See revision notes in 1 Pet 5:8, 1 Thess 5:6 |
| יְהוָה YHWH | Yahweh | the LORD, Jehovah | Renders the divine name as a name. Where the NT quotes an OT YHWH passage using *Kyrios*, the NT verse retains "Lord" to preserve the Greek; the OT source verse uses "Yahweh". |
| אָדָם *adam* | man / humankind (context) | — | Context-dependent per usage |

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.

## Change log for this document

Material changes to this document are themselves commits. Prior
versions of the stance are preserved in git history.

- **2026-04-21:** Removed creedal affirmations (Apostles' Creed,
  Nicene Creed, Chalcedonian Definition) and replaced with a
  theological-stance section that declines specific creedal
  commitment. Translation philosophy and contested-terms table
  preserved unchanged; those are methodology, not creedal
  commitment, and the project actually runs on them. Added a
  "Translating into other languages" section stating POB's long-
  term intention to ship in every feasible major language, with
  the full revision pipeline and transparent supported-language
  disclosure. Per-verse YAML citing the old `doctrine_reference`
  values is preserved as historical record; those are not
  retroactively edited.
context.ambiguity_review_standard: Apply the supplied DOCTRINE.md ambiguity policy: a defensible contextual rendering may be used in the main text when material alternatives and the reason for the choice are preserved in notes. A unique or uncontested interpretation is not required. Distinguish (a) an unreadable or unverified source, omitted content, invented restoration, or a construction for which no defensible English can be given, from (b) ordinary lexical, attachment, or referent ambiguity faithfully preserved in English or explained with viable alternatives. The former blocks publication; the latter does not automatically block it. A note cannot excuse unsupported wording: the proposed main rendering must itself be defensible from the supplied Greek. Clearly printed gaps must remain gaps, not be filled by invention. Never change a verdict merely to achieve acceptance.
context.selected_edition_coverage_standard: Coverage is assessed against ALL SURVIVING WORDING AND PRINTED GAP MARKERS in the selected image-checked edition, not against unavailable words of a hypothetical complete original. A confirmed printed lacuna must remain an explicit gap in the English, retaining the exact number of printed dots (layout whitespace may differ), with a source-quoted note explaining that its content is unavailable and no restoration has been supplied. Such faithful representation can pass selected-edition coverage; it must never be described as recovery of the lost wording or an unbroken original. Distinguish this from missing scan pages, unverified ink, omitted surviving Greek, an unsupported English completion, or a translation that obscures the gap: those remain blocking. Neither this scope clarification nor a prior suggestion is an instruction to accept a draft; independently check every surviving clause, every gap, and every disclosure.

passages.text: When Peter had said these things, the woman stopped and, as though from shock, fainted. Peter came over and paused, then urged her to recover a clear mind, trying to persuade her to say what exactly was happening to her. As though recovering from drunkenness, with the rest of her body gone limp, she regained control of herself so that she could bear the magnitude of the joy she was anticipating. Rubbing her face, she said, “Where is this young man?” Peter, who by now had discerned the whole situation, said, “You tell me first (for otherwise you have no way to see him)—.” In her eagerness she said, “I am the young man’s mother.” Peter said, “What is his name?” She replied, “Clement.” Peter said, “It is he. He was the one who spoke with me a short while ago, whom I instructed to wait for me in the ship.” Falling at Peter’s feet, she begged him to hurry to the ship. Peter said, “If you keep our agreement, I will do this too.” She said, “I will do everything; only show me my only child, for through him I will seem to see my two children who died here.” Peter said, “When you see him, remain quiet until we have left the island.” She said, “I will do so.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: stopped and, as though from shock, fainted
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπιστήσασα marks her coming to a halt, while ἀπέψυξεν here describes a collapse or loss of consciousness rather than literal death.

lexical_decisions.chosen: paused, then urged her to recover a clear mind
lexical_decisions.rationale: The absolute ἐπισχών can mean that Peter paused or waited; alternatively, the context may suggest that he supported or steadied her. νήφειν denotes recovering mental clarity.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἡ δὲ ὥσπερ ἐκ μέθης τὸ λοιπὸν τοῦ σώματος παρεθεῖσα
lexical_decisions.chosen: As though recovering from drunkenness, with the rest of her body gone limp
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐκ preserves the image of emerging from drunkenness, while the participial phrase depicts the remaining bodily weakness accompanying her recovery.

lexical_decisions.chosen: she regained control of herself so that she could bear
lexical_decisions.rationale: The unusual sequence presents her as recovering sufficiently to withstand the anticipated joy; more formally, she “turned herself back” so as to be able to endure it.

lexical_decisions.chosen: You tell me first
lexical_decisions.rationale: No object of “tell” is expressed. The translation preserves the incomplete prompt rather than supplying what Peter requires her to tell him.

lexical_decisions.chosen: If you keep our agreement
lexical_decisions.rationale: συνθήκας denotes agreed terms or conditions, referring to Peter’s requirement that she remain composed.

lexical_decisions.chosen: my only child
lexical_decisions.rationale: μονογενές presents Clement as her unique or sole remaining child in this context; “only-born child” would misleadingly conflict with the immediately mentioned deceased children.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: δόξω γὰρ δι’ αὐτοῦ τὰ δύο μου τὰ ἐνταῦθα τεθνηκότα ὁρᾶν τέκνα
lexical_decisions.chosen: for through him I will seem to see my two children who died here
lexical_decisions.rationale: δόξω with the infinitive is preserved as “I will seem to see,” expressing how seeing Clement will represent the two deceased children to her.

source_issues.source_quote: Εἰπέ μοι σὺ πρῶτον (ἄλλως γὰρ τοῦτον ἰδεῖν οὐκ ἔχεις) —.
source_issues.issue: The selected edition prints a terminal dash after Peter’s unfinished prompt and before the period. It may signal interrupted or deliberately incomplete speech, or it may be an editorial marker, but its function is uncertain. The marker is retained, and no unexpressed object or completion has been supplied.

passages.text: Peter therefore took her by the hand and led her toward the ship. When I saw him leading a woman by the hand, I laughed; and I came over and, out of respect for him, tried to lead her in his place. The moment I touched her hand, she gave a great cry like a mother, wrapped herself around me, and fervently showered me, her own son, with kisses. Knowing nothing of the whole situation, I was trying to shake her off as though she were mad; yet, feeling deference toward Peter as well, I was becoming irritated.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰς τιμὴν αὐτοῦ ἀντ’ αὐτοῦ χειραγωγεῖν αὐτὴν ἐπειρώμην
lexical_decisions.chosen: out of respect for him, tried to lead her in his place
lexical_decisions.rationale: Clement attempts to relieve Peter of the task as an expression of honor or respect.

lexical_decisions.chosen: she gave a great cry like a mother
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὀλολύζω denotes a loud, emotionally charged cry; the comparison explicitly characterizes it as maternal.

lexical_decisions.chosen: wrapped herself around me, and fervently showered me with kisses
lexical_decisions.rationale: περιπλέκομαι describes an enclosing embrace, while the intensive καταφιλέω conveys repeated or ardent kissing.

lexical_decisions.chosen: me, her own son
lexical_decisions.rationale: The accusative phrase stands in apposition to με and identifies Clement as her son from the mother’s perspective.

lexical_decisions.chosen: I was trying to shake her off as though she were mad
lexical_decisions.rationale: The imperfect depicts the ongoing or attempted action that Peter addresses with ἀποσειόμενος in the following section, rather than a completed dismissal.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: αἰδούμενος δὲ καὶ τὸν Πέτρον ἐπικραινόμην
lexical_decisions.chosen: yet, feeling deference toward Peter as well, I was becoming irritated
lexical_decisions.rationale: αἰδέομαι with Peter as its object expresses regard or deference; the imperfect ἐπικραινόμην describes Clement’s developing vexation.

passages.text: Peter said, “Let her be! What are you doing, child Clement, shaking off the woman who truly gave birth to you?” When I heard this, I became covered in tears; and I threw myself upon the woman who had borne me, who had herself fallen down, and showered her with kisses. For as soon as this was said to me, I somehow began dimly to recall her appearance. Many crowds therefore came running to learn about the woman who had been begging, saying to one another, “Her son, a man of distinction, has recognized her.” When we wished to leave the island at once with my mother, she said, “My longed-for child, it is right to say farewell to the woman who took me in. She is poor and completely disabled and lies at home.” When Peter heard this, he marveled, as did all the surrounding crowds, at the woman’s noble disposition. Peter immediately ordered some people to go and carry the woman in on a cot. And likewise, when the cot had been brought in and set down, Peter said in the hearing of all the crowds, “If I am indeed a herald of truth, then, as grounds for faith among those standing by, so that they may know that there is one God, the one who made the world, let her rise immediately in health.” As soon as Peter said this, the woman rose, having been healed. She fell before Peter, and after showering her familiar friend with kisses, she asked what this might mean. Her friend briefly related to her the whole event of the recognition, and those who heard it were astounded. Then the mother, seeing that her hostess had been healed, asked that she too might receive healing. Peter laid his hand on her and healed her as well.

lexical_decisions.chosen: shaking off the woman who truly gave birth to you
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὄντως emphasizes that she is genuinely Clement’s birth mother, while the present participle recalls his ongoing attempt to push her away.

lexical_decisions.chosen: I became covered in tears
lexical_decisions.rationale: περίδακρυς depicts Clement as streaming with tears.

lexical_decisions.chosen: I threw myself upon the woman who had borne me, who had herself fallen down
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participles distinguish the mother’s prior collapse from Clement’s movement toward and onto her.

lexical_decisions.chosen: I somehow began dimly to recall her appearance
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀμαυρῶς marks the memory as indistinct, and the imperfect suggests an emerging recollection.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to learn about the woman who had been begging
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἱστορέω here can mean to investigate, inquire about, or learn the story of someone; “to see” is also possible but expresses the crowds’ curiosity less fully.

lexical_decisions.chosen: completely disabled
lexical_decisions.rationale: The passive description indicates that her body has lost its strength or function; “completely paralyzed” is a possible narrower rendering.

lexical_decisions.chosen: some people to go
lexical_decisions.rationale: The indefinite pronoun refers to unspecified persons and does not identify their sex.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ ὁμῶς ἐνεχθείσης καὶ τεθείσης τῆς κλίνης
lexical_decisions.chosen: And likewise, when the cot had been brought in and set down
lexical_decisions.rationale: The explicit genitive τῆς κλίνης is most naturally the shared subject of both coordinated participles. A split attachment—“when she had been brought in and the cot had been set down”—is contextually possible but less source-transparent. ὁμῶς is retained as “likewise” rather than being replaced with ὅμως.

lexical_decisions.chosen: as grounds for faith among those standing by
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase presents the healing as serving or producing the faith of those present.

lexical_decisions.chosen: her familiar friend
lexical_decisions.rationale: συνήθης identifies Clement’s mother as the healed woman’s accustomed or close associate.

lexical_decisions.chosen: seeing that her hostess had been healed
lexical_decisions.rationale: Here ἱστορέω is understood as observing or ascertaining the hostess’s healed condition; “having inquired about the healed hostess” remains possible.

passages.text: And then, in this way, Peter spoke about God and the worship that belongs to him, adding at the end: “If anyone wishes to learn these things accurately, let him come to Antioch, where I have decided to remain for several days, and learn the things that lead to his salvation. For surely it cannot be that you know how to leave your homelands for commerce or military service and travel to distant places, yet are unwilling to undertake even a three-day journey for eternal salvation.” After Peter’s address, in the presence of the entire crowd, I gave the woman who had been healed one thousand drachmas for provisions and entrusted her to a certain good man who was the foremost citizen of the city and was naturally disposed to do this with joy. After also distributing money to many others and thanking the women who had once comforted my mother, I sailed across to Antaradus together with my mother, Peter, and the remaining companions; and in this way we made our way to our lodging.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the worship that belongs to him
lexical_decisions.rationale: διαφέρειν with the dative can denote what pertains or is proper to someone; θρησκεία here is religious worship or observance.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the things that lead to his salvation
lexical_decisions.rationale: πρός expresses relation or direction toward the hearer’s salvation.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐ γὰρ δὴ ἐμπορίας ἕνεκα ἢ στρατείας πατρίδας καταλιμπάνειν οἴδατε καὶ εἰς μακροὺς ἀπέρχεσθαι τόπους
lexical_decisions.chosen: For surely it cannot be that you know how to leave your homelands for commerce or military service and travel to distant places
lexical_decisions.rationale: The initial οὐ is retained as a rhetorical rejection of the inconsistent behavior Peter describes. Alternatively, the clause may be punctuated as a direct rhetorical question: “Do you not know how to leave ...?”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: διὰ δὲ αἰώνιον σωτηρίαν μηδὲ τριῶν ἡμερῶν ὁδὸν πορευθῆναι θέλειν
lexical_decisions.chosen: yet are unwilling to undertake even a three-day journey for eternal salvation
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering preserves the contrast and the negative force of μηδέ while expressing the syntactically abrupt infinitive θέλειν as part of the rhetorical rejection introduced by οὐ.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the foremost citizen of the city
lexical_decisions.rationale: πρῶτος describes the man’s leading civic standing, not merely his chronological position.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: φύσει μετὰ χαρᾶς τοῦτο ποιεῖν προῃρημένῳ
lexical_decisions.chosen: was naturally disposed to do this with joy
lexical_decisions.rationale: προαιρεῖσθαι here denotes settled willingness or inclination, qualified by φύσει.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to Antaradus
lexical_decisions.rationale: Antaradus is the conventional English form of the place-name Ἀντάραδος.

lexical_decisions.chosen: we made our way to our lodging
lexical_decisions.rationale: ξενία denotes guest lodging or quarters, and ὁρμάω here means to set out or proceed toward them.

source_issues.source_quote: διὰ δὲ αἰώνιον σωτηρίαν μηδὲ τριῶν ἡμερῶν ὁδὸν πορευθῆναι θέλειν
source_issues.issue: The infinitive θέλειν is syntactically abrupt where a finite verb would make the contrast straightforward. The verified supplied reading remains intelligible as an anacoluthon within the preceding rhetorical construction and has been preserved in translation.
source_issues.proposed_reading: διὰ δὲ αἰώνιον σωτηρίαν μηδὲ τριῶν ἡμερῶν ὁδὸν πορευθῆναι θέλετε

passages.text: When we had arrived ... and had partaken of food and given thanks as usual, while there was still time, I said to Peter, “My lord Peter, my mother performed an act of love for humanity when she remembered the woman who had hosted her.” Peter answered, “Do you really think, Clement, that the woman who bore you has performed an act of love for humanity, in that she repaid the woman who received her after the shipwreck? Or did you make this statement as one bestowing a great favor on your mother? If, however, you spoke not as one showing favor but as one telling the truth, you seem to me not to understand what the greatness of love for humanity actually is. It is affection for anyone at all, insofar as that person is human, without anything that naturally prompts it. Nor do I dare call the hostess who received the woman who bore you after the shipwreck a lover of humanity on that account. For, cajoled by pity, she had been persuaded to become the benefactor of a woman who had suffered shipwreck, was mourning children, was a foreigner, was naked, was alone, and was bitterly lamenting her disasters. Since she was amid so many disasters, who, even among the impious, would not have pitied her on seeing her? Consequently, even the hostess does not appear to have performed in this way an act of love for humanity, but to have acted under pity that had been stirred toward benefaction by countless disasters. How much more, then, did the woman who bore you—after acquiring abundant means and repaying her hostess—perform an act not of love for humanity, but of friendship? There is a great difference between friendship and love for humanity: friendship arises from repayment, whereas love for humanity, without anything that naturally prompts it, loves and benefits every human being insofar as that one is human. If, then, the hostess who showed pity had also pitied and benefited enemies who had wronged her, she would have been a lover of humanity. But if the enemy is a friend for some reason and the friend is an enemy for some reason, such a person is a friend or enemy of some particular cause, not of the human being.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: When we had arrived ...
lexical_decisions.rationale: γενομένων ἡμῶν can describe the party’s arrival or presence, but the printed lacuna removes its following specification; the three dots are retained without restoration.

lexical_decisions.chosen: an act of love for humanity
lexical_decisions.rationale: The expanded rendering preserves the etymological and argumentative connection among φιλανθρωπία, φιλάνθρωπος, and the later contrast with φιλία.

lexical_decisions.chosen: as one bestowing a great favor on your mother
lexical_decisions.rationale: Peter asks whether Clement’s judgment was an indulgent compliment to his mother rather than a true classification of her act.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἡ ἄνευ τοῦ φυσικῶς πείθοντος πρὸς οἱονδήποτε στοργὴ καθὸ ἄνθρωπός ἐστιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: affection for anyone at all, insofar as that person is human, without anything that naturally prompts it
lexical_decisions.rationale: Peter defines love for humanity as affection grounded solely in the recipient’s humanity, without a natural or circumstantial inducement.

lexical_decisions.chosen: For, cajoled by pity
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering retains the personifying force of κολακεύω: pity flatters, coaxes, or cajoles the hostess into action.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὑπὸ ἐλέου τοῦ ἐπὶ μυρίαις συμφοραῖς πρὸς εὐεργεσίας κεκινημένου
lexical_decisions.chosen: under pity that had been stirred toward benefaction by countless disasters
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive participle most naturally modifies ἐλέου, personifying pity itself as moved toward doing good by the accumulation of misfortunes.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἡ μὲν φιλία ἐξ ἀμοιβῆς γίνεται
lexical_decisions.chosen: friendship arises from repayment
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀμοιβή can mean repayment, return, or reciprocity; “repayment” keeps the immediate connection with the mother’s recompense to her hostess.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰ δὲ διὰ τί φίλη ἡ ἐχθρὰ καὶ διὰ τί ἐχθρὰ ἡ φίλη
lexical_decisions.chosen: But if the enemy is a friend for some reason and the friend is an enemy for some reason
lexical_decisions.rationale: διὰ τί may be interrogative, “why,” or causal, “for some reason.” The causal reading best continues the contrast between unconditional regard for a human being and attachment produced by a particular cause.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἡ τοιαύτη τοῦ τινὸς αἰτίου φίλη ἐστὶν ἢ ἐχθρά, οὐ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου
lexical_decisions.chosen: such a person is a friend or enemy of some particular cause, not of the human being
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering preserves the source’s compressed genitive contrast. Alternatively, it may mean that such a person is friend or enemy because of some particular cause, not because the other is human.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.
